title: How Buffett buys businesses: Berkshire's 1995 letter on GEICO, float, moats and acquisitions
summary: Buffett explains why he distrusts most acquisitions yet loves buying great businesses with great managers, using Helzberg's, R.C. Willey and the full GEICO purchase. He also covers insurance float economics, retail versus have-to-be-smart-once businesses, and his own mistakes.

principles.text: Compare every acquisition against buying small pieces of the best public businesses; this discipline stops expansion-driven deals.
principles.quote: Our practice of making this comparison - acquisitions against passive investments - is a discipline that managers focused simply on expansion seldom use.

principles.text: Having no strategic plan is an advantage: you aren't forced toward silly purchase prices.
principles.quote: Even so, we do have a few advantages, perhaps the greatest being that we don't have a strategic plan.

principles.text: Ignore sellers' projections; sellers know more and choose the timing, when the business is walking fine.
principles.quote: In any case, why potential buyers even look at projections prepared by sellers baffles me. Charlie and I never give them a glance

principles.text: Look for economic castles protected by unbreachable moats; rock-bottom operating costs widened GEICO's.
principles.quote: In business, I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable "moats."

principles.text: Float is only valuable if it costs less than the market price of money; low-cost float acts like equity.
principles.quote: An insurance business is profitable over time if its cost of float is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds.

principles.text: Accept lumpy but higher long-term returns instead of smooth ones, since most managers opt for smoothness.
principles.quote: In other words, we prefer a lumpy 15% to a smooth 12%.
